title: Safety Patrol Boys and a Missing Pledge

place.label: Site of Portola Junior High (now Martin Luther King Jr. Middle School), Bacon Street at Goettingen

hook: At Portola Junior High, boys drilled as traffic patrols, pupils dug gardens, and one Bayview girl was left craving the end of a pledge nobody recited any more.
story: In the 1930s Portola Junior High School stood at Bacon and Goettingen, on the site of today's Martin Luther King Jr. Middle School. A photograph from the decade shows its Safety Patrol traffic boys marching in formation across the yard [1]. Another, captioned 'Burrows & Brussels', shows children and adults gardening at the school [1]. Pupils came from well beyond the Portola. Ruth Eshow Upton went to Bret Harte Grammar School on Third Street in the Bayview, then followed her classmates to Portola Junior High [2]. At Bret Harte, every morning ended with the Pledge of Allegiance and then a second pledge, 'I am a California Child'. When she moved up to the seventh grade at Portola she was surprised to find the class simply stopped after the national pledge. It left, she wrote, 'an unfinished feeling', like putting down an apple or cookie with one bite left and then not being able to find it [3]. Decades later she found the California pledge's full lyrics on the website of Johnson Park Elementary School in Marysville, though nobody there knew who wrote it [3].

title: Lucky Lager Tavern Becomes the White Palace

place.label: White Palace, 1524 Silver Avenue at San Bruno Avenue

hook: A 1934 tavern changed its name when the Lucky Lager Brewery opened nearby, lost its building to a freeway, and lives on as a corner deli known for crab sandwiches.
story: The White Palace on the corner of Silver and San Bruno began as a bar. According to the family who ran it, it opened in 1934 as the Lucky Lager Tavern and became the White Palace Tavern in 1936, when the Lucky Lager Brewery opened a few blocks to the south [1]. A 1943 photograph shows patrons inside [1]. When the old building was torn down for the new 101 freeway, the business moved across the road [1]. A deli counter came later. Ray's parents started it in 1979, Ray began working there at 14, and he took over in 2000 with his brother-in-law Charles [1]. The city's business register lists White Palace Liquor at 1524 Silver Avenue from 2000 [2]. By 2012 the sandwiches, nearly all around five dollars, drew workers from the Silver Avenue Family Health Center across the road, who came in for crab and avocado. One of them told the Portola Planet about the day the owners stepped in when a customer started making racist remarks to another [1]. Ray was also proud of scoring 100 out of 100 on health inspections, and of a city award for consecutive perfect scores [1].

title: Storytime at the Portola Playground

place.label: Palega Recreation Center (then Portola Playground), near Felton and Hamilton streets

hook: Long before Palega got its glass wing, a costumed storyteller gathered Portola children on the grass of what everyone then called the Portola Playground.
story: Around 1935 an unknown photographer, in pictures now tagged 'Recreation & Parks', visited the Portola Playground near Hamilton and Felton streets, the park now called Palega. One picture shows children sitting on the lawn with a house behind them, and a woman in costume who seems to be the director telling a story. Another, looking north toward Bernal Heights, shows a woman reading to a cluster of small children. A couple of the same kids appear in both [1]. Four years earlier, a Spring Valley Water Co. photographer recorded children on Felton Street between Bowdoin and Hamilton on 24 July 1931, watching a trenching machine dig the ditch for a 48-inch University Mound water pipeline [2]. The old name lasted a long time in local memory. When a group of women who met at St. Elizabeth's grammar school in 1968 walked their childhood haunts in 2017, one of their stops was 'Portola Park (now Palega, but still Portola to us)' [3].

title: Bocce, Sodas and Sofas on The Road

place.label: San Bruno Avenue near Woolsey Street, by the Avenue Theatre

hook: Streetcar photographers caught a vanished San Bruno Avenue: Blondi's Bocci Ball, a soda fountain, a sweet shop and a coffee shop, all within sight of the Avenue's marquee.
story: Photographers who came to San Bruno Avenue for its streetcars also caught the shops around them. On 12 March 1947 one looked north near Woolsey Street at Muni H-line car #926. On the right is a business called Blondi's Bocci Ball, with the Avenue Theatre behind [1]. Around 1949 another, at Bacon Street, looked north across San Bruno to the Avenue and captured Lido Pastry and the Jolly Joan Fountain, while an H-line car went by with 'Enlist now - U.S. Coast Guard' painted on its side [2]. In May 1968 the Avenue was showing 'The Jungle Book', and a view south from near Burrows took in Leonard Supermarket, Fenech's Furniture, Hagi's Coffee Shop, Ampel Interiors, the Avenue Sweet Shop and Lido Pastry [3]. People remembered these places for a long time. In 2014, when the Breakfast at Tiffany's space sat empty, a commenter named Josie wished for a coffee shop again. She meant a real restaurant 'like Breakfast at Tiffany's or our so missed, Ave Sweet Shop', and asked who else remembered Sparta's restaurant [4].

title: Seven Preschoolers in a Church Basement

place.label: The San Francisco School, 300 Gaven Street

hook: The San Francisco School started with seven Montessori preschoolers under a Woolsey Street church, then bought a building on Gaven Street.
story: In March 1966 five parents and four teachers signed the articles of incorporation for the San Francisco Montessori School. It opened in a church basement on Woolsey Street in the Portola with seven preschool pupils, and parents and teachers shared the leadership [1]. In 1969 the school bought 300 Gaven Street and added a first grade. By the 1970s it ran to fifth grade with 145 students, and the lower school's camping trips and last-day ice skating had begun. In the 1980s it reached eighth grade and renamed itself The San Francisco School [1]. Head of school Terry Edeli retired in 2008 after 35 years of service [1]. The school stayed in the neighbourhood as it grew. In 2012 its sixth graders adopted Gaven Street from Barneveld to Bowdoin under the city's Adopt-A-Street programme, and collected more than 1,000 cigarette butts in a few hours [2]. That June it was due to break ground on a $9 million gym and theatre. Head of school Steve Morris said it was named a Community Center because 'we wanted its use to go beyond our gates' [3].

title: The Portola Girls of St. Elizabeth's

place.label: Former St. Elizabeth's School (now Alta Vista School), 450 Somerset Street

hook: Ten girls met at St. Elizabeth's grammar school in 1968. Fifty years later they talked their way back into their old classroom, now a tech-founded science school.
story: In 1968 ten girls met at St. Elizabeth's Catholic grammar school, beside the church whose sidewalks run along Somerset, Wayland and Goettingen [3], and stayed friends for the next fifty years [1]. They graduated in 1975 and called themselves third-generation San Franciscans and 'Portola Girls'. On 17 November 2017 several of them came back to walk the neighbourhood. Rosanne Field, born Rosie Maffei, organised it after visiting the Sweeny Street house she grew up in, where her brother still lives [1]. Three of them grabbed a bite at Tiffany's on San Bruno, where her father's photo had once hung on the wall under the name 'Rocky'. The group took photos in front of their childhood homes, and passing E.R. Taylor they shouted for a friend who was inside teaching [1]. The school they got into had changed. In 2012 Alta Vista School, a science- and maths-focused private school founded by Abdur Chowdhury, a former chief scientist at Twitter, moved into the old St. Elizabeth's School at 450 Somerset. It took over more than 25,000 square feet [2]. The friends still 'weaseled' their way into their old classroom and told the teachers about their Catholic-school high jinks [1].

title: Christmas Lights All Year at Tiffany's

place.label: Breakfast at Tiffany's, 2499 San Bruno Avenue

hook: After 35 years the San Bruno Avenue diner closed when its chef died. Regulars mourned his hash browns and Stella By Starlight, and still it came back.
story: Breakfast at Tiffany's served breakfast and lunch at 2499 San Bruno Avenue from 1978 [1][2]. The city's business register lists Gerald A. Adan there from 1993 until 6 October 2013 [3]. That month the diner closed after Adan, its owner and chef, died. His sister April taped an emotional note to the windows thanking loyal customers, and said she hoped whoever came next would keep some of its classic American style [1]. The comments were full of small details. The bathrooms had Christmas lights all year round. One family missed the 'Stella By Starlight' and the breakfast croissant, and remembered watching Gerald 'do' the spuds in the back, saying no one made hash browns like him [1]. The building, which also had a dentist upstairs, went on the market for $895,000 [2]. The diner did come back. Healthy Breakfast Inc. registered Breakfast at Tiffany's at the same address in March 2014 [3]. In 2017 a group of women who grew up in the Portola began their reunion with a bite at 'Tiffany's', glad it had 'stood the test of time' [4].

title: Sopes from Jalisco on San Bruno

place.label: La Placita Mexicatessen, 2531 San Bruno Avenue

hook: Juana Perez from Jalisco ran a no-frills Mexicatessen on San Bruno Avenue for nearly three decades, and it was the only place in the Portola for sopes.
story: The city's business register shows Juana R. Perez opening La Placita Mexicatessen at 2531 San Bruno Avenue on 5 May 1984 [1]. When the Portola Planet's lunch reviewers came in June 2012, she told them she was from Jalisco and had run the place on San Bruno for 29 years, a year or so more than the register shows [2]. There were no frills. The walls held pictures of Chivas, the Guadalajara football club, and photographs of Mexican towns and countryside. Mexican candies and snacks lined the counter, and the fridge had Jarritos beside harder-to-find bottles like Cuzcatlán Cola Champagne [2]. Perez said La Placita was the only place in the Portola where you could get sopes, served with crunchy radishes on top. The empanadas were fried, and goat birria was a weekend special [2]. Carl Nolte had noted in 2009 that San Bruno Avenue had 'a couple of Mexican restaurants' on a street where Chinese restaurants now filled old Italian dining rooms and the Lido Pastry had become a Central American bakery [3]. Perez's registration ends in February 2013. New owners registered the same name and address the following month [1].

title: Roast Duck Where Italians Once Dined

place.label: Wing Hing Restaurant, 2550 San Bruno Avenue

hook: By 2009 Chinese lions guarded San Bruno Avenue doorways that once led to Italian dinners. At Wing Hing, the dish missing from the English menu was ginger-garlic frog.
story: By 2009 about half of the Portola's roughly 13,000 residents were Asian, and on San Bruno Avenue, Carl Nolte wrote, 'Chinese lions guard the entrance to restaurants that once served Italian food' [1]. Wing Hing was one of the Chinese restaurants on the street. Its owner, Flora Luo, told the Portola Planet in 2012 that it had opened in 1994. The city's register records the business at 2550 San Bruno from 1996 until 2022 [2][3]. At lunch the place was packed. In the evenings most orders were takeaway, phoned in and picked up by locals. Many families bought a pound of roast duck or pork from the window for under $10, had it chopped on the spot and built a home meal around it [2]. The head chef, whom Luo called Sifu, or 'master', could take a duck apart in seconds at the front of the shop. Then came the one dish, Luo said, that was unique to Wing Hing and not on the English menu: frog stir-fried with garlic and fresh ginger. Luo said it was 'very high in nutrients and often drunk with a beer' [2].

title: Drag Queen Bingo and Body Slams

place.label: El Toro nightclub, 2470 San Bruno Avenue

hook: A Latin dance club where Sinatra supposedly once sang became the Portola's queer stage, with drag bingo, marriage-equality 'brides' and a drag queen carried out of a wrestling ring.
story: El Toro is a Latin music and dance club on San Bruno Avenue. Local legend says Frank Sinatra once sang there, when it was Fucile's Bar [1]. In July 2015 the club hosted Ricky Lips, billed as one of Mexico's best-known divas. Two days later the Portola Neighborhood Association held a Drag Queen Bingo fundraiser there: a $6 cover, $2 off for anyone in drag [2]. By 2017 the bingo was a semi-annual fundraiser for local projects [1]. At one, the marriage-equality activists John Lewis and Stuart Gaffney came in drag, John in one of activist Molly McKay's wedding dresses. Outside afterwards, a woman on her way to the bus gasped, 'How beautiful! Your wedding day!' [1]. In November 2017 pro wrestling arrived. At the first 'SF Slam', a contender attacked the drag queen Pollo Del Mar, and in the storyline she was carried from the ring [3]. Pollo, the stage name of Paul Pratt, told the Chronicle he lived on the outskirts of the Excelsior, which he called 'very heterosexual, very diverse, very blue-collar' [4].

title: 'No More Chinese' Became 'Love More Chinese'

place.label: Palega Recreation Center, 500 Felton Street, where neighbours rallied

hook: One September morning the Portola woke to racist graffiti on homes and shops. Within hours neighbours had painted hearts over the hate.
story: On the morning of 7 September 2015, residents found the words 'No More Chinese' sprayed on homes and businesses in several parts of the Portola [1][2]. Six years earlier the Chronicle had counted about half of the neighbourhood's residents as Asian [3]. People reacted fast. Within hours residents had turned the slogan into '[heart] more Chinese' [1]. Public Works crews answered 311 calls and cleaned the walls quickly, and Captain Vaswani of the Bayview police station opened a hate-crime investigation [2]. The Portola Neighborhood Association called a community meeting at Palega Park for that Thursday evening, and neighbours were urged to knock on doors and bring the people next door [2]. A few days later a large, mixed crowd rallied at one of the graffiti sites. It was led by Supervisor David Campos and the association's president Chris Waddling, an immigrant gay man whose husband is Chinese American [1]. The vandal turned out to be a long-time resident. He was prosecuted and convicted of multiple counts of vandalism and hate crimes, and by 2017 there had been no repeat [1].

title: Irene Crescio's Lilies on San Bruno Avenue

place.label: San Bruno Avenue commercial corridor, near Bacon Street

hook: A lifelong Portolan and 38-year phone-company worker walked San Bruno Avenue almost daily, tending its lilies, reporting graffiti and pushing the city for street-tree lights.
story: Irene Crescio spent her whole life in the Portola. She was the daughter of Mario and Elide Crescio and worked for 38 years at Pac Bell [1][2]. Into her eighties she sat on the board of the Portola Neighborhood Association, and she took San Bruno Avenue as her own project [1]. She worked with the city to bury the street's power lines and plant trees along it. She also lobbied for electrical outlets on the streetlights, which were later used for the decorative tree lighting she had imagined [1]. She walked the avenue almost every day, looking after the lilies and reporting graffiti and burnt-out lamps to the city [1]. She died peacefully in her sleep on 26 January 2016. Her funeral Mass was at St. Elizabeth Church, Somerset at Wayland [1][2]. Her family asked that, instead of flowers, people give to the neighbourhood association or to the Good Shepherd Gracenter on Bacon Street [1]. Later that year her memorial fund helped pay for a new multimedia mural in the neighbourhood [1].

title: Twenty Back Gardens, One Beer

place.label: Ferment Drink Repeat brewery, 2636 San Bruno Avenue

hook: A San Bruno Avenue nanobrewery handed hop roots to neighbourhood gardeners, then brewed their harvest into a 'Hyper-Local Fresh Hop Ale'.
story: Ferment Drink Repeat registered as a business in October 2013, and at 2636 San Bruno Avenue from May 2016 [1]. The nanobrewery project had been under way for almost two and a half years, through a long wait for city approvals, when the taproom had its soft opening on 25 May 2016 [2]. It opened with four beers: San Bruno Saison, Ole Black, Orange is the New Black and the Inauguration Session IPA. Dogs were welcome, and so was takeaway food from other San Bruno Avenue restaurants [2]. In March 2017 the owners, Kevin and Shae Inglin, worked with Ruth Wallace, who ran the Portola Garden District tour. They handed hop rhizomes to more than 20 neighbourhood gardeners, who set up an email list to share tips, photos and progress [3]. The first harvest was small, 10 pounds of buds, but enough for four barrels (eight kegs) of Kevin's 'Hyper-Local Fresh Hop Ale', poured at the Garden Tour after-party [3]. Two Portola residents writing in the Bay Times called it a 'queer-friendly microbrewery' and noted plans for a special Pride brew [4].

title: The Woolsey Street Cemetery

place.label: 309 Woolsey Street, between Brussels and Goettingen

hook: Two Halloweens running, a neighbour turned the side yard of a little 1890s Victorian into a graveyard made from found objects, complete with 'missing doll' posters.
story: In October 2016 a Portola Planet writer walking to the bus on the 300 block of Woolsey Street began to notice odd things. First came a poster for a missing doll, asking anyone who found it to return it to the 'Woolsey Cemetery' [1]. Then the 1890s Victorian perched above the street changed. A doll's head was nailed to its gate with a 'Happy Halloween' greeting, and a ghostly figure sat silently on the garden stairs [1]. In the gap between the Victorian and the bungalow next door was a small cemetery with joke tombstones, skeletons and body parts [1]. The next Halloween the display at 309 Woolsey was back and even bigger, with eerier lighting, rubber rats and personalised tombstones. Its maker was neighbour Larry Winum [2]. Unlike most Halloween displays, nothing was bought from a shop. Winum built everything from found objects, down to a candlelit woman hunched on the front steps. On Halloween night he planned to hand out candy to any children brave enough to stop by [2].
